title: Documentary Director: There Is No Typical Old Age, Only Specific People
dek: Fan Shiguang, who shot two seasons of Qianlang (前浪), says most marriages end up lukewarm or worse, and growing old together to the very end is rare as hen's teeth; what we lack most isn't stories, it's money, and the habit of seeing old people as specific human beings.
why: The first half is the two hosts talking, more feeling than information; the second half is the director interview, packed with killed story pitches and behind-the-scenes detail, noticeably denser — worth starting at 41 minutes.
who: Listeners following aging, caregiving, family institutions and documentary craft; people in elder care, insurance, legal services and content who can treat the back-half director interview as a story-selection methodology.
skip: 0:11-3:53 opening setup and impressions; you can start straight from the inheritance story at 4:08.

points.h: Five million in inheritance, and the law fights the deathbed wish
points.body: An elderly woman with no close family died in a Shanghai nursing home. While alive she had made an advance guardianship notarization with notary Li Chengyang, but left no will. Sorting her belongings, the notary found she had left five million in assets, including a house, cash and passbooks. She had said orally, many times, that she wanted to donate it to society and not give it to relatives, but that wish had no legal form. Li Chengyang ultimately chose to follow the law and look for statutory heirs, tracing through archives to children and relatives she had not seen in years. There was disagreement inside the notary office too; some colleagues thought her wish should simply be respected. The compromise was to propose to the inheriting children that 200,000 of the five million go to a fund helping old people with no one to rely on. The children agreed.

points.h: Whether they slept together decided whether the inheritance could go
points.body: An elderly man with a terminal illness gave his advance guardianship and his estate to a woman who had cared for him for years and was not a relative — and he had a biological daughter. The notary office argued fiercely over it, and one key point was whether the two slept together: if they did not, the caregiver was merely a nanny or a live-in housekeeper, and an old man leaving his estate to his nanny was morally acceptable; if there was a sexual relationship, it stopped conforming to propriety. The caregiver was herself married, but had had no contact for years, so in effect the marriage did not exist. So it became an open-relationship question, and the notary office did not want to bear the risk of indecency over such a judgment.

points.h: Older people finding partners increasingly skip the marriage certificate
points.body: Li Kangmei, the subject of episode two, was with Lao Li for eighteen years without ever registering the marriage, and there was no de facto marital relationship. The hosts found this far more common than they had imagined: after divorce or the loss of a first marriage, many older people entering a new relationship choose not to marry. They don't necessarily say they love this person; they say they want someone to keep them company, someone to take care of them — behind it a fairly deep need against loneliness. Lao Li already had a terminal illness, and Li Kangmei's choice was whether to stay to the last moment or leave early because there was no de facto marital relationship.

points.h: Reality TV forces you to pick a side every five minutes
points.body: The hosts contrast documentary with reality TV: much of the tension in reality TV is manufactured, backed by a very strong narrative — knowing the audience looks down on mama's boys, they'll fabricate a mama's boy on screen. This destroys the audience's tolerance for the complexity of real intimate relationships: every plot beat, every five minutes, demands a stance, and that stance must be the morally correct one, then projected onto some character, and wherever that character goes you're on his side. Documentary does the reverse: it shows that no one has it easy, some characters get more screen time and some less, but you can see everyone's difficulty, and quite a few of them appear pixelated and anonymous.

points.h: The old generation says I sleep badly, not I'm depressed
points.body: Medical anthropologist Arthur Kleinman found that young people today have a rich psychological vocabulary and can quickly say I'm depressed, I'm anxious, I'm a bit bipolar; but the older generation, even when expressing psychological needs, still uses somatized language — I've been sleeping badly lately, I have a bit of a headache — and won't say I sleep badly because I think too much, that I'm a little depressed. The hosts explain: in our culture it's easier to talk about physical pain, anyone can have a headache or a fever, there's no stigma; the moment you talk about depression or anxiety, it's a different order of stigma and pain.

points.h: The pitch he killed: she just wanted to play mahjong
points.body: Director Fan Shiguang tells a story he killed himself: the most diligent auntie in a hospice ward, whose husband had bladder cancer and not long to live. She took the bus in at seven or eight every morning and left at five or six at night, like going to work, but you could see no love on her face — she just asked the doctors and nurses over and over how much longer other people's family members had. Only later did he learn her son had died of a heart attack two years earlier; she was a shidu family, a family that had lost its only child, and her tears had probably run dry two years before. Someone asked what she wanted to do after her husband died, and she said she wanted to play mahjong, because he had never let her play. The first scene shot after the husband died was her finding workers to smash the legs off a two-meter bed with a sledgehammer, one by one, and buying a mahjong table to put in that spot. The story was never used, because the team couldn't find her real inner world — they only had part of the facts.

points.h: Growing old together is rare as hen's teeth, not the norm
points.body: Fan Shiguang says the team embedded in roughly fifty families during fieldwork, and across two seasons found that going from youth all the way to growing old together to the very end is not the norm but rare as hen's teeth; most marriages are lukewarm, or worse. He tells of the first season's episode Lovers: an old man with Alzheimer's loses control and hits his wife; the daughter forcibly sends him to a specialized nursing home; the old woman sneaks off to visit every few days, and the hospital won't let her come because it affects his mood. After the old man is sent to hospital, gravely ill, the old woman finally gets her chance to wait on him — cutting his nails, washing his hair, washing his feet. A month or so after he dies, she says through tears: I looked down on him my whole life. When I was young I was a good student and he was a poor one; my family were intellectuals and his were workers; he insisted on courting me, and I had no way out, and in the end I muddled through a whole life with him.

points.h: Learning to drive at 95: one sentence stripped her of her rights
points.body: Fan Shiguang says the team worked hard to break stereotypes, because people love to sort into groups and stick on labels — old people are like this, they're just confused — and there is deep prejudice in that. In season one there was a 95-year-old man learning to drive and taking the license test. Fan caught himself saying instinctively, "driving is all very well, but he is 95 after all," and then asked himself: in that sentence of mine, 95-year-olds are stripped of their rights — as if he doesn't deserve it. Public Security Ministry regulations never said a 95-year-old can't learn to drive, but in that verbal violence the right was stripped away. The episode's bullet comments were full of: can this old man really drive on the road, so selfish, what if he hits someone — and all those worries rest on prejudice.

quotes.text: Whether they slept together — they slept together. Why is this detail key? Because if they didn't sleep together, this caregiver is merely, say, a nanny to this elderly man with a terminal illness, or a live-in housekeeper, that kind of role, and the old man wanting to leave his estate to the nanny seems acceptable, in terms of moral propriety. But if there is a sexual relationship between the old man and the caregiver, all at once it stops conforming to propriety.
It's as if every plot beat, every five minutes, I need to have a stance, and that stance is utterly unshakable, it must be the morally correct one.
She'll say I've been sleeping badly lately, she'll say I have a bit of a headache, but she won't say I sleep badly because I think too much, that I'm a little depressed or that I'm overly anxious.
She said I want to play mahjong. People asked why. She said he never let me play mahjong before.
From youth all the way to truly growing old together, making it to the very end is not the norm, it's rare as hen's teeth — making it to the end. Most marriages are lukewarm, or even bad.
He said, when I was young I was a good student, he was a poor student; my family circumstances were good too, his family were workers, we were an intellectual family.

I asked myself: 95-year-olds, in that sentence of mine, are actually stripped of their rights — as if he doesn't deserve it. Public Security Ministry regulations never said a 95-year-old can't learn to drive, but in our verbal violence, I stripped away his rights.
Once you have this label, all these people get sorted into a prison — you lock them all into a prison, and word after word, it's all a kind of violence.
